title: The Lampstand, the Olive Trees, and the Spirit
summary: In the fifth vision the angel wakes Zechariah to see a golden lampstand with seven lamps fed by two olive trees. The meaning is given as a word to Zerubbabel: the temple will be finished not by might nor by power but by God's Spirit, and the hands that laid its foundation will complete it. The two olive trees are the two anointed ones who stand beside the Lord of all the earth.
story: The previous vision cleansed Joshua the high priest. This one turns to Zerubbabel, the governor from David's line, who was leading the temple rebuilding. It sits at the center of the eight visions, and its message is the heart of the whole series: the work God has begun will be completed by his Spirit. For a small community with few resources, surrounded by suspicious neighbors and dependent on a distant Persian king, that word answered the real fear that the project was too big for them. The temple would in fact be finished about four years later, in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15).
historical:
Zerubbabel had laid the foundation of the temple years before, soon after the first return from exile (Ezra 3:8-11), and had resumed the work in 520 BC at the urging of Haggai and Zechariah (Ezra 5:1-2). Around this time the Persian governor of the province Beyond the River, Tattenai, came to ask who had authorized the building and wrote to Darius about it (Ezra 5:3-17). Darius searched the royal archives, found Cyrus's decree, and ordered that the work continue with funds from royal taxes (Ezra 6:1-12). The great mountain of verse 7 has been read as the obstacles in general, as the heap of rubble on the temple site, or as the opposition of powerful enemies; each fits the situation, and the prophet does not name it.

The complaint about the day of small things (verse 10) reflects what Haggai 2:3 and Ezra 3:12 also record: the new temple seemed poor and small to those who remembered Solomon's.
cultural:
The lampstand (Hebrew menorah) was a familiar piece of temple furniture. The tabernacle had a single golden lampstand with seven lamps (Exodus 25:31-40), and Solomon's temple had ten (1 Kings 7:49). The lampstand Zechariah sees is different: it has a bowl on top feeding the lamps, and it is supplied directly by living olive trees, so that it never has to be refilled by human hands. Olive oil was the fuel of every lamp in the ancient Near East and also the oil used to anoint priests and kings.

The capstone and the plumb line belong to ancient building rites. In Mesopotamia, rebuilding a temple involved formal ceremonies, including the careful laying of stones or bricks that linked the new building to the old, and texts from the region describe the king's personal part in them. Zechariah's picture of Zerubbabel bringing out the top stone to shouts of grace, grace, and holding the plumb line (literally the stone of tin), fits that world. The exact meaning of the stones in verses 7 and 10 is debated, but the scene is a ceremony marking stages of the temple's building.
literary: The vision is interrupted. Zechariah describes the lampstand and asks what it means (verses 1-5), but before the angel explains the olive trees, the text inserts a word of the LORD to Zerubbabel (verses 6-10a), and only then returns to the explanation (verses 10b-14). Many scholars think the oracle was placed inside the vision deliberately, so that the lampstand's meaning is the Spirit's power to complete the temple. The exchange do you not know what these are? No, my lord occurs twice (verses 5 and 13), slowing the reader down. The seven eyes of the LORD that scan the whole earth (verse 10) link back to the seven eyes on the stone in 3:9.

outline.t: Fifth vision: the golden lampstand and two olive trees
Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit
Zerubbabel will finish the house: the day of small things
The two anointed ones beside the Lord of all the earth

doctrines.note: The key verse of the chapter sets God's Spirit against military might and human strength. The lampstand burns because it is fed without human effort, and the temple will be built the same way. The Spirit is God himself at work, supplying what his people cannot.
The seven eyes of the LORD range through the whole earth. Nothing escapes his sight, and small beginnings are not beneath his notice; he rejoices to see the plumb line in Zerubbabel's hand.

The day of small things is not to be despised, because the hands that laid the foundation will complete it. Hope rests on God's promise to finish what he has begun, and the capstone is brought out to shouts of grace, acknowledging the finished work as his gift rather than the builders' triumph.

words.note: Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. The word can mean moving air, the breath of life, or the Spirit of God. In verse 6 it stands against might (chayil, usually the strength of an army) and power (koach, personal strength), and it names God's own active presence as the force that will complete the work.

Menorah, lampstand. The word names the seven-branched lamp of the tabernacle and temple, which gave light in the holy place before God. Zechariah's lampstand, fed by living trees, has often been read as a picture of God's people, or of the temple community, shining by oil supplied by God.

Chen, grace or favor. The shout in verse 7 repeats it, grace, grace, to the capstone. The word describes kindness freely given by a superior. It will appear again in 12:10, where God pours out a spirit of grace and prayer.

Yitshar, fresh olive oil. The phrase translated the two anointed ones in verse 14 is literally the two sons of fresh oil. Oddly, it uses the word for oil as a product of the harvest rather than the usual word for anointing oil, so some scholars think it stresses fruitfulness and blessing rather than anointing in the formal sense.

christ: The two anointed ones are most often identified with Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor, the priestly and royal leaders who stand in God's service, and the pairing prepares for chapter 6, where priest and king come together in the Branch. The New Testament shows that both offices meet in Christ, the anointed one (which is what Messiah and Christ mean), who is both priest and king. Revelation 11:4 takes up this chapter's imagery for two witnesses who are the two olive trees and the two lampstands, and the risen Christ walks among lampstands that are his churches (Revelation 1:20). The promise that God's house will be built by his Spirit rather than by human power runs through the New Testament's picture of the church as a temple being built by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:21-22). The link is thematic: the chapter does not predict Jesus, but its pattern of God's work completed by his Spirit through his anointed servants finds its fullest form in him.

hard.q: Who are the two olive trees, the two anointed ones?
hard.a: Most interpreters take them to be Joshua and Zerubbabel, the priest and the governor who lead the community, since the previous chapter concerned Joshua and this one concerns Zerubbabel. Some scholars point out that neither man had been formally anointed as far as we know, and that the unusual phrase sons of fresh oil may describe them as channels of God's blessing rather than as anointed officials. A few have suggested the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. Christian readers have sometimes taken the two trees as the two Testaments or, following Revelation 11, as two future witnesses. The chapter's own emphasis falls less on who they are than on where they stand: beside the Lord of all the earth, serving him.

questions: Where are you tempted to measure what God is doing by might and power, by money, numbers, or force?
Who has despised the day of small things? What small beginning in your life or church might God be pleased with?
The lampstand burned because it was fed from living trees. What does it look like to depend daily on God's supply rather than on stored-up strength?
